title: Scientific Investigation
standard_text: Learners plan and carry out fair tests, identify variables, make predictions, collect and record data in tables and graphs, calculate averages, and draw conclusions supported by evidence. (summary of the MATATAG Science curriculum, Grade 5, Quarter 1: Materials)
meta_desc: Free Grade 5 Science worksheets (MATATAG, Quarter 1: Materials): fair tests, variables, predictions, tables and graphs, averages and conclusions. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Change one thing and keep the rest the same.
key_sub: A conclusion must match the evidence.
body_html:
How to think about it

A scientific investigation answers a question by testing. In a fair test, you change only one variable (the independent variable), measure another (the dependent variable), and keep all other variables the same (controlled variables).

Record results in a table and show them in a graph. Repeat trials and find the average. Look for patterns and write a conclusion that the data support; explain any results that do not fit.

Example

Testing which ball bounces highest: what must stay the same?

Fair test

Answer: the drop height and the floor

Example

Results 10, 12, 14 cm. Average?

Add and divide by 3

Answer: 12 cm

Common mistakes

  • Changing two things at once.
  • Writing a conclusion from one trial.
  • Ignoring results that do not fit without explaining them.

items.q: What is a fair test?
c: a test where only one variable is changed and the others are kept the same
items.e: Change one thing.

items.q: Why do scientists repeat a test several times?
c: to check the results are reliable
because the first result is always wrong
items.e: Repeated results that agree are more trustworthy.

items.q: What should you do with an anomalous result?
c: repeat the test or leave it out of the mean
items.e: It may be a mistake.

items.q: Which is the safest way to heat water in a classroom test?
c: on your own with a candle
holding a glass over a flame

items.q: What is an anomalous result?
c: a result that does not fit the pattern of the others
items.e: Check it or repeat it.

items.q: Which is an observation, not a conclusion?
c: Ice always melts fastest in foil.
The ice in the foil cup melted after 20 minutes.
items.e: An observation is what you saw or measured.

items.q: Is this an observation or an inference (an explanation)? “Wool traps air, so it slows down heat moving into the ice.”
c: a prediction made before the test
items.e: An observation is what you saw or measured; an inference explains it.

items.q: Investigation: “Does the length of a lever affect the force needed to lift a load?” What should be kept the same to make it a fair test?
c: the force needed to lift the load
the same load and the same pivot position
items.e: Control variables keep the test fair.

items.q: Is this an observation or an inference (an explanation)? “The water in the black bottle reached 40 °C.”
c: a prediction made before the test
items.e: An observation is what you saw or measured; an inference explains it.

items.q: A class investigates how the temperature of water affects how fast a stock cube dissolves. Which variables should be controlled (kept the same)?
c: the same amount of water and the same kind of stock cube
the same marble and the same push
items.e: Change: the temperature of the water. Measure: the time to dissolve. Keep the same: the same amount of water and the same kind of stock cube.

items.q: A class investigates how the thickness of an elastic band affects how far it can stretch. Which variables should be controlled (kept the same)?
c: the same length of band and the same mass hung on it
the same amount of water and the same kind of stock cube
items.e: Change: the thickness of the band. Measure: how far it stretches. Keep the same: the same length of band and the same mass hung on it.

items.q: Investigation: “Does the number of spoons of bicarbonate of soda affect how much a balloon inflates?” Which variable should be changed?
c: the same amount of vinegar and the same size of bottle and balloon
the number of spoons of bicarbonate of soda
items.e: Change one variable: the one in the question.

items.q: Investigation: “Does the type of surface affect how far a toy car rolls?” Which variable should be changed?
c: the same car, the same ramp height and letting go without pushing
items.e: Change one variable: the one in the question.

items.q: A class investigates how the type of surface affects how far a marble rolls. Which is the independent variable (the one you change)?
c: the same marble and the same push
items.e: Change: the type of surface. Measure: the distance the marble rolls. Keep the same: the same marble and the same push.

items.q: Is this an observation or an inference (an explanation)? “The seedling grew tall and pale because it was looking for light.”
c: a prediction made before the test
items.e: An observation is what you saw or measured; an inference explains it.

items.q: A class investigates how the amount of salt in water affects how fast bean seeds sprout. Which variables should be controlled (kept the same)?
c: the same kind of seed and the same temperature
the same lamp and the same wires
how many days the seeds take to sprout
items.e: Change: the amount of salt. Measure: how many days the seeds take to sprout. Keep the same: the same kind of seed and the same temperature.

items.q: Investigation: “Does the length of a lever affect the force needed to lift a load?” Which variable should be changed?
c: the force needed to lift the load
the same load and the same pivot position
items.e: Change one variable: the one in the question.

items.q: Investigation: “Does the temperature of water affect how fast salt dissolves?” What should be kept the same to make it a fair test?
c: the same amount of salt and water, and stirring the same way
the time for the salt to dissolve
items.e: Control variables keep the test fair.

items.q: A class investigates how the thickness of an elastic band affects how far it can stretch. Which is the independent variable (the one you change)?
c: the same length of band and the same mass hung on it
items.e: Change: the thickness of the band. Measure: how far it stretches. Keep the same: the same length of band and the same mass hung on it.

items.q: Investigation: “Does the amount of sunlight affect how tall a sunflower grows?” What should be kept the same to make it a fair test?
c: the same seeds, soil, pot size and amount of water
the height of the sunflower after three weeks
items.e: Control variables keep the test fair.

items.q: A class investigates how the size of a parachute affects how long it takes to fall. Which variables should be controlled (kept the same)?
c: the time it takes to fall
the same amount of water and the same time in the sun
the same drop height and the same load
items.e: Change: the size of the parachute. Measure: the time it takes to fall. Keep the same: the same drop height and the same load.

items.q: Investigation: “Does salt water make iron nails rust faster than tap water?” What should be measured?
c: the same kind of nail, the same amount of water and the same place
how much rust forms in a week
items.e: Measure the result (the dependent variable).

items.q: Is this an observation or an inference (an explanation)? “The seedling in the cupboard was pale and 9 cm tall.”

items.q: Which unit would you use to record the volume of water in a cup?

items.q: A group measured the number of seeds that sprouted in each tray three times: 13 seeds, 12 seeds, 14 seeds. What is the average?
items.e: Add the results and divide by 3: 39 ÷ 3 = 13.

items.q: A group measured the time for an ice cube to melt in the sun three times: 25 min, 23 min, 24 min. What is the average?
items.e: Add the results and divide by 3: 72 ÷ 3 = 24.

items.q: Which type of graph is best for showing which material kept a drink warmest?
items.e: Bar chart: separate groups. Line graph: change over time or a continuous measurement. Scatter graph: a link between two measurements.

items.q: Which type of graph is best for showing the mass and length of 20 different fish?
items.e: Bar chart: separate groups. Line graph: change over time or a continuous measurement. Scatter graph: a link between two measurements.

items.q: Which unit would you use to record the mass of a rock?
items.e: Electronic scales measures it in g.

items.q: A group measured the distance a toy car rolled off a ramp three times: 109 cm, 99 cm, 104 cm. What is the average?
items.e: Add the results and divide by 3: 312 ÷ 3 = 104.

items.q: A group measured the temperature of water in a shaded bottle at 3 pm three times: 24 °C, 23 °C, 22 °C. What is the average?
items.e: Add the results and divide by 3: 69 ÷ 3 = 23.

items.q: Which equipment would you use to measure the mass of a rock?
items.e: Use electronic scales; it measures in g.

items.q: Which equipment would you use to measure the length of a leaf?
c: a trundle wheel or long tape measure
items.e: Use a ruler; it measures in mm.

items.q: Which type of graph is best for showing the favorite fruit of learners in a class?
items.e: Bar chart: separate groups. Line graph: change over time or a continuous measurement. Scatter graph: a link between two measurements.

items.q: A group measured the time for sugar to dissolve in warm water three times: 74 s, 76 s, 72 s. What is the average?
items.e: Add the results and divide by 3: 222 ÷ 3 = 74.

items.q: A group measured the height a tennis ball bounced three times: 62 cm, 56 cm, 59 cm. What is the average?
items.e: Add the results and divide by 3: 177 ÷ 3 = 59.

items.q: Which type of graph is best for showing the height of a sunflower measured every week?
items.e: Bar chart: separate groups. Line graph: change over time or a continuous measurement. Scatter graph: a link between two measurements.

items.q: Which equipment would you use to measure the volume of water in a cup?
c: a trundle wheel or long tape measure

items.q: Which type of graph is best for showing the temperature of a cup of tea every 2 minutes as it cools?
items.e: Bar chart: separate groups. Line graph: change over time or a continuous measurement. Scatter graph: a link between two measurements.

items.q: Which type of graph is best for showing the number of birds of each kind seen in a garden?
items.e: Bar chart: separate groups. Line graph: change over time or a continuous measurement. Scatter graph: a link between two measurements.

items.q: Which equipment would you use to measure the time for a marble to roll down a ramp?
c: a trundle wheel or long tape measure
items.e: Use a stopwatch; it measures in s.

items.q: Which equipment would you use to measure how bright a flashlight is?
c: a trundle wheel or long tape measure
items.e: Use a light meter; it measures in lux.

items.q: Which unit would you use to record the width of the school oval?
items.e: A trundle wheel or long tape measure measures it in m.

items.q: What does it mean if a conclusion is 'supported by evidence'?
c: It was guessed before the test.
items.e: Evidence-based.

Which conclusion is supported by Emmanuel's results?
c: The smaller the pieces, the faster the sugar dissolved.
items.e: A conclusion must match the results and not go beyond them.

items.q: Which is the best way to share the results of a test with the class?
c: a clear table and graph with a short conclusion
drawing a picture of the equipment only
items.e: Communicate results so others can check them.

items.q: Nico measures how long a candle burns under jars of different sizes. Why should an adult light the candles?
c: to make the candles burn longer
to keep everyone safe from burns
items.e: Safety is part of planning.

items.q: Kyla's results: ramp 10 cm, car rolls 40 cm; 20 cm, 80 cm; 30 cm, 120 cm. Predict the distance for a 40 cm ramp.
items.e: Each 10 cm of height adds 40 cm of distance.

items.q: Which change would make Trisha's plant test fairer?
c: giving every plant the same amount of water
putting some plants inside and some outside
using a different pot for each plant
items.e: Keep everything the same except the variable you test.

items.q: Which conclusion matches the data: 'the bigger the jar, the longer the candle burned'?
c: The jars were the same size.
Bigger jars hold more air, so the candle could burn longer.
Small jars make candles burn longer.
items.e: A conclusion explains the pattern.

items.q: How could you make timing a falling parachute more accurate?
c: drop it from a greater height and take the mean of several tries
items.e: Longer times and repeats.

items.q: Kenneth finds one result much bigger than the others. What should he do?
c: Repeat that test to check it.
items.e: An anomalous result should be checked.
